articles.title_orig: Stocks, Nasdaq Futures Climb as AI Trade Rebounds: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks, Nasdaq Futures Climb as AI Trade Rebounds: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day.
In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory.
Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%.
Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55.
SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59%
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off.
"The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification."
But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent."
"Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said.
The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India.
Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative."
"European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending."
U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities.
But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."

articles.title_orig: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.title_zh: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.content_orig:
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.
One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.
The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.
PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.
In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.
Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.
It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.
But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.
Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.
This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.
In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.
In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.
After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".
However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".
Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.
Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May . The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.
If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

articles.title_orig: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.title_zh: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A new wave of tariffs from the White House would move overall rates almost exactly back to where they stood in early 2026, according to one initial analysis of the new duties.
The Yale Budget Lab says the newly unveiled plans , if enacted, would return the US to rates seen just before the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's blanket tariffs in February.
Read more: 5 ways to tariff-proof your finances
The estimated overall average statutory rate would rise from the current 11.4% to 13.9% early next year. The rate in February, just before the high court struck down Trump's tariffs enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 (IEEPA), was 13.8%.
That remains well below the overall rates seen in 2025. The group estimates that 2025 rates exceeded 15%, peaking at nearly 23% in the weeks after "Liberation Day" in April 2025.
"The administration said it wanted to rebuild the IEEPA tariff regime using Section 301; with this proposal, it will have done so in the aggregate," the group said in its analysis.
The mix of countries bearing the duties will shift slightly, the budget lab noted, with apparel, electronics, and appliances among the biggest categories affected by the new duties.
The reaction from other corners, meanwhile, was that a combination of widespread exemptions, smaller rate changes on other trading partners, and many tariffs that will not be stacked meant the impact could be smaller.
"The latest US tariff announcement is not as alarming as it looks," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, wrote in an analysis.
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year," he added, noting that an exact projection from his group will come later on.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer downplayed the macroeconomic effects in a CNBC appearance Wednesday, describing the total changes as moves that "really will just top up a few percentage points."
He added that the higher rates on China — the one place where the new tariffs are set to stack on top of other tariffs — are an exception and that the situation for most countries will be less dramatic.
One major trading partner dodged new tariffs this week when it was announced that an investigation in Mexico was still being reviewed. Greer added that recent talks have been going well.
Canada was also not subject to this eight-month investigation, which wrapped up this week and covered China, the European Union, and 14 other nations.
China is set for a 20% baseline "deal rate," which could jump to 40% if ongoing talks break down, while other partners will see much more modest changes.
Rates on some EU goods will jump from 10% to 15% if the new tariffs on excess structural capacity go forward and replace previous tariffs imposed around the issue of forced labor.
Yet the exemption for an array of goods that the EU and others enjoy includes key products such as semiconductors, as well as automobiles, steel, and aluminum, which are subject to a separate tariff authority.
Other goods the Trump administration has carved out in recent months, notably certain energy and food products, will also be exempted.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Oil prices inch back up as Iran and its Houthi allies escalate threats and attacks
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Oil prices inch back up as Iran and its Houthi allies escalate threats and attacks
articles.content_orig:
The body of a Jordanian sailor who was reported missing after an Iranian attack on his vessel in the Strait of Hormuz last week, was found off the coast of Ras Al Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday .
"The body of Mohamed Hossam al-Din al-Otaibi , may he rest in peace, was found on Wednesday," the ministry said.
The United Arab Emirates' state-owned ADNOC energy company reported the sailor missing last week after one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. It said 11 crew members were injured in the attack.
The Jordanian ministry praised the efforts of UAE and Omani authorities for locating the sailor's body.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Thursday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers were on fire after striking sea mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz via southern shipping lanes the U.S. military insists are safe, but Tehran has repeatedly warned vessels to avoid.
"Since the early hours of today, two non-compliant oil tankers have exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines north of the port of Khasab," which is on the Omani coast in the center of the strait, Iranian state media quoted the IRGC as saying.
The report, which was not immediately corroborated by independent maritime agencies, said one of the ships was a supertanker laden with more than 2 million barrels of crude oil that was left burning after hitting a mine.
The statement — the latest in a series of daily claims by the Iranian regime of ships striking mines in the strait —   came after IRGC Navy commander Rear Adm. Ali Azmaei reiterated Tehran's warning to shipping firms that passage through the strait would only be safe "by respecting Iran's sovereignty."
"We not only have control of this waterway, but have also placed the power to change the equations at the heart of the Strait of Hormuz," declared Azmaei, whose remarks were also carried by state media.
Ship transits through the Strait of Hormuz have fallen again this month and the amount of crude oil and other products shipped outside the Persian Gulf remains at just over half of pre-war levels, according to data from shipping intelligence company Kpler.
The number of ships making the journey per week fell from 217 to 147 between Nov. 1 and Nov. 23, Kpler said in two reports this week.
Tanker crossings averaged 11 per day for the week ending Nov. 21, compared to 50 per day before the war, meanwhile, though the company noted that many crossings are "dark," or done with their AIS transmission systems turned off, usually for safety reasons.
The International Maritime Organization has recorded 141 attacks on commercial ships in and around the strait since the war began in February, including at least 15 in November. October was the worst month for attacks on vessels in the region since the war began, with at least 35 ships coming under attack according to the IMO.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations agency said late Wednesday that it had received a report of an explosion near a tanker about 50 nautical miles west of Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, west of the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
The tanker's master reported an explosion, which UKMTO attributed to an "unknown projectile," but the vessel was not damaged and there was no environmental impact, UKMTO said in an advisory .
Iran claimed earlier Wednesday, without offering evidence or details, that a liquified natural gas carrier had struck a sea mine in the southern part of the strait — the latest in a series of similar daily claims.
Iran insists all vessels must use northern shipping lanes through the strait, and only with authorization from its military. The regime said Wednesday that it was tightening its control over the vital waterway, which the U.S. military insists is safe and open to traffic.
Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they had targeted the Saudi ports of Jeddah and Jazan in response to Saudi strikes on a Yemeni port controlled by the Iran-backed group as their conflict further escalated.
The attacks came after the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had struck Yemen's Red Sea port city of Hodeida, drawing threats of retaliation from the Yemeni fighters.
"Both operations resulted in damage to the targeted sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.
An explosion was later heard in Saudi capital Riyadh, according to an AFP journalist and residents, after authorities issued an alert warning of a "hostile aerial threat," which was lifted shortly after.
Residents in northern and eastern Riyadh confirmed hearing the blast, with one saying their house windows "shook violently."
Saudi forces said air defenses destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward the capital by the Houthis, as well as a cruise missile in the western part of the country and a drone near Jeddah's port.
Turki al-Malki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition battling the Houthis, said no civilian injuries resulted from the debris of the intercepted drone.
In recent weeks, the Houthis has launched a barrage at Saudi targets including the financial district, airports, energy infrastructure and military sites.
The Saudi coalition has in turn been striking Houthi-held areas of Yemen in support of the internationally-recognized government, which has been battling the Houthis for territory since a civil war reignited in July.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry has called out Republican Sen. John Cornyn for a post on X criticizing Iran's alleged pursuit of nuclear weapons, however, the quote cited by the senator was actually about North Korean nuclear ambitions.
The Texas senator cited International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi raising concern "about a rapidly built extension at the Yongbyon gas centrifuge uranium enrichment plant."
Cornyn wrote on X, "Doesn't sound like the Iranian regime is giving up on its nuclear weapons aspirations."
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei correctly pointed out Grossi was speaking about Yongbyon, North Korea, and nothing to do with Iran.
Cornyn serves on the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, one of the governing body's most important posts. Cornyn is on his way out of the Senate. He was soundly defeated by Ken Paxton in the Republican primary this spring. Paxton would eventually lose earlier this month to Democrat James Talarico.
The post on X remains live 24 hours after the senator shared it.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Israel was trying to drag the United States into another war after an Israeli minister alleged Tehran is building chemical weapons.
"This warmonger shamelessly accuses Iran ... of developing and concealing such heinous weapons in pharmaceutical factories. The objective is audacious: to deceive the US into fighting yet another war on its behalf," he wrote in a statement posted on X .
Israel has for years accused Iran of trying to acquire nuclear weapons, but Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Tuesday alleged Tehran is building chemical weapons and vowed to stop the Islamic republic from obtaining them.
"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons but has not yet reached the capability to attack Israel with them," said Katz in a statement published by his Likud party on Telegram. He also left open the possibility of preemptive strikes against Iran.
"We must not allow this to proceed," he said.
President Trump mentioned the same thing to Fox News earlier this month on his Asia trip, saying, "Well, there is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear. ... Nuclear is much harder, and they're looking at gas and they're looking at the bio, the biological weapons."

articles.title_orig: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.title_zh: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.content_orig:
Germany 's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro- Iranian terrorist group.
It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne , several hours' drive to the north.
Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.
Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing.
Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization.
They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran .
Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025."
Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks."
"On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out."
Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency , the BfV.
More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation.
Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention.
One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it.
The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran.
These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9 , which caused property damage but no injuries.
Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later . An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after , prompting heightened security across the Netherlands.
In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March , not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism.
Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

articles.title_orig: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.title_zh: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.content_orig:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings.
It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations.
The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S.
The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.
“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said .
James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).
Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.
Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement . “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig speaks to reporters outside federal court in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Nov. 24, 2026. Larry Neumeister—AP
Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.
Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.
The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.
The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.
The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.
The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China .
Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.
The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.
Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.
The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.
Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October

articles.title_orig: Lured by High Salaries, Some Brazilians Were Duped Into Fighting for Russia
articles.title_zh: Lured by High Salaries, Some Brazilians Were Duped Into Fighting for Russia
articles.content_orig:
Russia is recruiting citizens of Indonesia and the Philippines into its armed forces under the guise of civilian employment, with some foreign workers being sent to fight against Ukraine after arriving in Russia, according to a Bloomberg on November 24.
Moscow has intensified its recruitment efforts across Southeast Asia amid a shortage of military personnel for its war against Ukraine, targeting men seeking employment abroad, particularly those facing financial difficulties.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Prospective recruits are promised one-time payments of up to $35,000 upon signing military contracts, as well as monthly earnings of up to $3,000.
Recruiters advertise lucrative civilian employment opportunities in logistics, security, construction, and administration through social media. Some men arrive in Russia believing they have secured jobs in the hospitality industry or other civilian sectors, only to learn that they have unknowingly signed military service contracts.
Bloomberg noted that recruitment agents, human trafficking networks, and fraudulent recruitment operations are exploiting the vulnerability of migrant workers seeking economic opportunities abroad.
The recruitment practices have prompted authorities in both Indonesia and the Philippines to take measures aimed at protecting their citizens.
Indonesian police are investigating suspected recruitment cases as potential human trafficking offenses where there is evidence of deception or coercion into military service.
Jakarta has also urged Moscow to add Indonesia to its list of countries whose nationals are excluded from Russian military recruitment. Whether Russia has responded to the appeal remains unknown.
Meanwhile, the Philippines has stepped up efforts to combat fraudulent overseas employment schemes. With the assistance of Philippine authorities, up to 250,000 social media posts linked to such job offers have been removed.
According to Bloomberg, citing Ukrainian military figures, Russia recruited 128 Philippine nationals during the first nine months of 2026 alone.
The recruitment of foreign nationals comes amid emerging evidence of the scale of losses among foreigners serving in the Russian military.
A joint investigation by NEST Centre and Dossier Centre has identified 6,947 death records of foreign nationals believed to have been killed while fighting for Russia during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The investigation draws on a hacked database from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, containing approximately 11.6 million death records registered between 2021 and September 2026, with Central Asian nationals accounting for the majority of the identified cases—4,091 deaths, or 58.9% of the total sample.

articles.title_orig: China and other U.S. trading partners hit back at Trump's new tariff plans
articles.title_zh: China and other U.S. trading partners hit back at Trump's new tariff plans
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and President Trump speak to reporters aboard Air Force One. Photo: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity.
Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns.
Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of  a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs are a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed, a senior U.S. official said.
Between the lines: The administration proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place.
The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers.
What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations.
Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .

articles.content_orig:

Donald Trump spent the opening moments of the Thanksgiving holiday reading negative news stories about himself before moaning about them on social media.
In a Truth Social post sent at 12:47 a.m. ET, the 80-year-old president raged at David E. Sanger, The New York Timesâ White House and national security correspondent, calling him a âmediocreâ reporter and a âlowlife.â
The post came hours after Sanger published a damning article noting that Trump takes credit when the stock market risesâas seen following the presidentâs extraordinary intervention to demand that Nvidia reinstate sex-mad Jensen Huang as CEOâbut takes no responsibility when his decisions or policies contribute to a downturn.
The 80-year-old president has a habit of staying up all night scrolling on social media.
âDavid E. Sanger, the mediocre reporter for the Failing New York Times, didnât mention in his recent story on me the successful closing of the Border, best crime stats in years (lowest murder rate since 1900 - 126 years!), biggest Tax and Regulation Cuts, EVER, the most successful naval blockade in history, the destruction of Iranâs Navy and Air Force (and more!), the ONE DAY WIN against Venezuela, and todayâs big success in straightening out the Obama caused mess in Iowa,â Trump posted.
âDavid Sanger is a lowlife that only writes what he is told to write by his bosses. Also, until the Election, best Market, EVER, 82 days, settled 8 Wars, and the USA is respected again like never before!â
In his article, Sanger noted that Trump took credit for Nvidiaâs stock surging more than 31 percent after the announcement that Huang would return as the companyâs CEO, even after he admitted having multiple affairs, including with one woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
Donald Trump excitedly likened Nvidiaâs stock price to a ârocket ship going in the right directionâ after Jensen Huang returned as CEO.
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Trump, who owns around $62 million worth of Nvidia stock , admitted he had âconvincedâ the Nvidia board to bring Huang back and assured its members that his extramarital affair did not pose a national security risk, making the president around $15 million on his stock holdings in the process.
However, the bump was short-lived, with Nvidiaâs stock falling 5.9 percent on Tuesday and another 5 percent on Wednesday, as uncertainty over Trumpâs controversial intervention involving Huang and fears of an AI bubble bursting weighed on investors.
In a Wednesday Truth Social post, the president tried to blame the stock marketâs decline on the midterm election results, in which Democrats swept control of the House and Senate as voters rejected Trump and the GOP across the country.
âI wasnât on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-kâs, would be BOOMING. I told you so!!!â Trump wrote.
Sanger noted that during both of Trumpâs terms, the president had cited stock market performance as proof of his business acumen and his status as the âmaster of the many intersections between the presidency and economic performance.â
âBut Mr. Trump has also made it clear that he does not subscribe to the theory that if a president is responsible for market surges, he must also be responsible for declines,â Sanger added.
The Daily Beast has contacted The New York Times and David E. Sanger for comment.

articles.title_orig: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
articles.title_zh: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
articles.content_orig:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.
SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.
Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.
"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.
Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.
It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".
It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".
Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."
The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.
New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

articles.title_orig: China firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs
articles.title_zh: China firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs
articles.content_orig:
China on Thursday said it firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including China, and urged Washington to correct its course and resolve the issue through dialogue and consultation.
Speaking at a news conference in Beijing, Ministry of Commerce spokesman He Yadong said China would closely follow developments and reserve the right to take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.
He described the US investigations as “a typical act of unilateralism”, saying they seriously undermine the international economic order and violate World Trade Organization rules.
ALSO READ: China's high-tech FDI surges 31.3% in first 10 months
The Office of the US Trade Representative on Nov 25 released the findings of its investigations into alleged manufacturing overcapacity and proposed additional tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
“Some countries are pursuing protectionism in the name of addressing overcapacity, politicizing normal market competition and turning industrial development issues into political tools,” He said.
He said such measures would leave those countries’ structural problems unresolved, destabilize global industrial and supply chains, disrupt industrial cooperation and push up global inflation.
They would also harm businesses and consumers and pose long-term, systemic risks to global economic growth, he added.
On July 28, the Ministry of Commerce released a position paper on so-called overcapacity, calling for a comprehensive and objective assessment of global industrial capacity and for greater international cooperation.

articles.title_orig: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.title_zh: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: Shein agrees to pay $100 million to settle claims of misleading customers
articles.title_zh: Shein agrees to pay $100 million to settle claims of misleading customers
articles.content_orig:
Fast-fashion retailer Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle Federal Trade Commission allegations that it misled customers.
The FTC says the money will be used to compensate customers harmed by the company's practices.
The agency said tens of thousands of customers reported receiving their orders late, while others never received them at all. Shein allegedly failed to notify customers of shipping delays as required by law.
RELATED STORY | Fashion giant Shein facing new scrutiny from US regulators
The FTC also accused Shein of publishing positive product reviews while suppressing or deleting negative ones.
Investigators also found that some cotton Shein advertised as U.S.-grown originated in China.
Under the proposed settlement, Shein would be required to stop misrepresenting delivery times, suppressing negative reviews and making deceptive claims about its supply chain. The company would also have to provide adequate customer service.

articles.title_orig: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
articles.title_zh: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.
The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.
The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.
Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.
On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.
China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said.
Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.
On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue."
He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.
The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls.
The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December.
"While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler said.
Washington has warned that tariffs on Chinese goods could double to 40% if the USTR finds that Beijing is not engaging. "If the trade war did start up again, today's measures provide the U.S. with some ammunition," Williams said.
Even the sweeping actions against the other 13 trading partners appear aimed squarely at China, said Williams, who tallied that the word "China" appears 253 times in the USTR's report on Vietnam, and 315 times in the document on the European Union.
"Foremost among the 'unreasonable acts, policies, and practices' that these countries are criticised for is being slow to restrict imports and FDI from China," Williams said.
While the proposed tariffs generally lift average rates only modestly, India and Vietnam stand out because of the wider gaps between the rates they would face with and without a deal, analysts said.
India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall sharply to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks with the U.S. produce reciprocal trade agreements.
The two countries have "a strong incentive" to conclude deals with Washington to secure the lower rates, Cutler said.
Vietnam's trade ministry said Thursday that it was working with the U.S. to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, according to Reuters . India could also gain an edge over some Asian rivals through comparatively lower levies if New Delhi concludes its long-pending trade deal with Washington.
Singapore faces a similar challenge. The proposal sets a maximum potential rate of 20% on its exports, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, which could fall to 10% if it reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. or concludes other negotiations addressing the USTR's findings, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry .
The ministry said it disagreed with the findings and was "very disappointed" with the proposed action, arguing that it failed to account for the structure of Singapore's economy.
Under the U.S.-Singapore Free Trade Agreement, Singapore imposes zero tariffs on U.S. goods, while the U.S. has run a trade surplus with the city-state for more than 20 years, the ministry said. That surplus grew to $33 billion in 2025 from $27 billion in 2024.
Singapore said it would submit further comments during the public consultation period and urge the USTR to reconsider.
Exemptions for semiconductors and other electronics should cushion the impact on South Korea and Taiwan, whose economies are heavily concentrated in those sectors, analysts said.
The USTR singled out South Korea for its concentration in memory-chip production and what it described as outsized government support. Yet it excluded the country's chips from the proposed excess-capacity tariffs.
Taiwan, which faces an excess-capacity tariff cap of 15%, also benefits from exemptions for other electronics, including mobile phones and networking equipment. Its effective tariff rate would rise to about 9% from 6%, Williams estimated.
— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
articles.title_zh: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.
Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights resumed again about 90 minutes later.
The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.
The ground stop came on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.
Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.
At 21:41 local time, the FAA confirmed that "flights will be resuming shortly".
Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.
The Miami-Dade area is also under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.
A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

articles.title_orig: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.title_zh: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Chinese consumer rights advocate Wang Hai has spent three decades exposing counterfeit goods and seeking compensation for buyers. In recent months, he left China fearing he was a target of the authorities, but now he is stranded in South Korea with his family, facing possible deportation home.
Wang, a well-known campaigner against counterfeit goods, said China invalidated his passport and South Korean authorities rejected his asylum. The United States also revoked his tourist visa, narrowing his options for leaving South Korea and deepening his fears of being sent back to China.
Chinese authorities launched a campaign against organized crime in July, saying they would target “malicious compensation claims.” Since then, authorities have arrested at least 100 people for allegedly extorting businesses through anti-counterfeiting work or consumer compensation claims, according to official statements reviewed by The Associated Press.
Wang said the arrests made him fear he could be next, prompting him to leave a country where official Chinese media had once praised him for his role as anti-counterfeiting activist.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press it was not aware of Wang’s case. The Ministry of Public Security did not respond to a request for comment.
The quagmire in which Wang, 53, and his family have found themselves has drawn concerns from rights advocates over China’s efforts to target critics abroad and the narrowing options for people seeking refuge in the U.S.
“The Chinese government’s practice of transnational repression is well documented, including in South Korea,” said Yaqiu Wang, senior China researcher at Human Rights Watch, based in Washington , and “there is no doubt that the Trump administration has created a far more hostile environment for immigrants, and even visitors.”
Wang spoke to the AP from South Korea about his situation and has appealed the rejection of his asylum application in that country.
The activist fears he will end up in jail if deported to China
The activist said that he arrived in South Korea in late September with his wife, 8-year-old daughter and infant son.
Wang said he believed Chinese authorities were targeting him and that dozens of his staff members were arrested and questioned. Some remain in detention, he said. One staffer had his passport revoked while traveling from Thailand to Singapore last month, according to him.
“The very same job has suddenly morphed from being praised into something associated with organized crime — it’s absolutely surreal," said Wang.
Asked what he is afraid of if he is sent to China, Wang didn’t hesitate: “I would definitely spend the rest of my life behind bars.”
A notice reviewed by AP showed South Korean immigration authorities rejected Wang's and his family's applications for refugee status. AP also reviewed the U.S. Embassy email that revoked his visa, in which U.S. authorities told Wang that new information made him inadmissible to the U.S. or ineligible for a U.S. visa but did not provide specific details.
The U.S. State Department didn't immediately respond to the request for comment.
He was once praised as a ‘woodpecker’ rooting out fraud
Wang became a household name in China in the 1990s for exposing counterfeit goods, an increasingly widespread problem as the country’s market economy expanded rapidly and consumer protection oversight lagged.
In 1998, Wang joined a roundtable discussion with then-U.S. President Bill Clinton during his visit to Shanghai. Wang told Clinton he had been viewed as “immoral” at home, according to a White House transcript.
Chinese state media, however, largely portrayed him favorably, calling him “China’s No. 1 anti-counterfeiting activist.” Professional consumer advocates were compared to “woodpeckers,” rooting out problems in the marketplace.
Wang ran a rights-protection company in Beijing for about 30 years and a testing laboratory supporting anti-counterfeiting work for five years. He said both were forced to close after many of his staff, including three lawyers, were arrested in September.
The closure of his offices came after China launched its campaign against organized crime. Authorities said some people were using consumer complaints, lawsuits or threats of exposure to extort money from businesses through what officials called “malicious compensation claims.”
Some lawyers say consumer rights advocates play a positive role by exposing illegal practices, pressing businesses to address problems and helping authorities enforce regulations.
“The fact that some individuals engage in these activities as a profession or as a source of income does not invalidate the legitimacy of such social oversight itself,” said Zhang Yansheng, a Beijing-based lawyer.
After fleeing China, Wang seeks a new home with freedom
Wang’s consumer advocacy began more than three decades ago, when he suspected two pairs of Sony headphones he bought at a Beijing department store were counterfeit. He bought the remaining 10 pairs and secured compensation of twice the purchase price. It was widely celebrated on Chinese state media as a pioneering case of consumer activism.
He went on to run his own company and testing lab, helping consumers seek compensation and pushing for stronger consumer protections.
Wang and other advocates also pushed for a minimum compensation payment of 500 yuan ($75) for consumers, a proposal later incorporated into a revised consumer protection law in 2013.
His most recent case involved helping cherry farmers in the northeastern city of Dalian get compensation after they bought fake pesticide. He said Dalian police later arrested and detained around four dozens of people including the cherry farmers, two lawyers who represented the farmers, and Wang's staff.
Wang said he has since focused on researching asylum options and hopes to settle in the U.S., Canada, Britain, Australia or New Zealand, seeking what he called “real law enforcement and freedom” to “get away from China's transnational repression.”
After his U.S. visa was revoked, Wang is seeking resettlement in Canada with the help of a human rights organization.
Fearing arrest by Chinese authorities even outside China, he said he and his family mostly stay indoors in South Korea. He said his bank accounts in China have been frozen, leaving the family in financial difficulty, and his 8-year-old daughter is struggling with her mental health because she cannot attend school.

According to Magyar, Zelensky presented him with an August 1942 issue of the Transcarpathian weekly Az Őslakó (“The Native”).
The Hungarian prime minister said he had often spoken about his great-grandfather, Lajos Eryős, who served as chief notary of Oroszvég during World War II. The former village, known in Ukrainian as Rosvyhovo, is now part of Mukachevo.
The issue contained an announcement of his great-grandfather’s appointment to the post. Magyar said the gesture held special significance within the context of diplomatic protocol.
“Needless to say, a personal gift of this kind has special significance in diplomatic protocol,” Magyar wrote.
On behalf of the Hungarian people, Magyar presented Zelensky with a painting of Mukachevo Castle by Attila Kopriva, a Hungarian-born Transcarpathian artist, and a book by Kyiv-based artist, restorer, and researcher Árpád István Magyar, also known as Stefan-Arpad Yosypovych Magyar. The book is titled Hungarians in Kyiv: From the 9th Century to the Present — Chapters in the History of Hungarian-Ukrainian Relations.
As reported, Magyar arrived in Zakarpattia on November 24 for his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister. In Uzhhorod, he and Zelensky laid flowers at the memorial to fallen Ukrainian defenders on the Hill of Glory.
The Ukrainian president and Hungarian prime minister also met with representatives of the Hungarian community in Zakarpattia.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth, Pentagon officials floated using wartime law to reappoint Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: Hegseth, Pentagon officials floated using wartime law to reappoint Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth considered using a Cold War-era law to justify the U.S. government stepping in and forcing Nvidia to reinstate its scandal-hit CEO Jensen Huang , according to a report.
The Washington Post claims Hegseth and his senior deputy Steve Feinberg discussed the prospect of President Donald Trump using the Defense Production Act of 1950 to compel the chipmaker’s board of directors to bring back Huang, a step it did eventually take Monday without the act being invoked.
Hegseth and Feinberg reportedly argued that Huang’s return, following his November 12 resignation after a number of extramarital affairs came to light, was essential to national security given that the U.S. is currently locked in an arms race with China to win dominance of AI .
The Pentagon, however, has pushed back on the report and denies Hegseth made any such a proposal.
The emergency act in question grants the president broad authority to intervene in the private sector in the interest of protecting the economy and has been used in the past to gain control of production lines to supply the military during wartime.
The first Trump administration used it during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020 to order General Motors to produce ventilators with which to treat coronavirus patients.
“Essentially they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects,” one administration official cited by the Post said.
It is not clear whether the idea of using the DPA to force Nvidia’s hand ever reached Trump and Vice President JD Vance – who weighed in on Huang’s behalf in the hope of restoring calm to the financial markets – or was ever put to the company, according to the newspaper.
However, a Pentagon official told the Post : “The conversations described between DOW [Department of War] senior leaders never happened and no such proposal was made by the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, or Under Secretary.”
The Independent has also reached out to the department for comment.
The president has admitted he and Vance played a pivotal role in persuading the Nvidia board to bring back the 63-year-old, its leader since 1993, who was forced to step down earlier this month when his infidelities were exposed, one of which was with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believed to be a Chinese spy .
Nvidia likewise admitted in a statement it had received input from “senior levels” of government before making its U-turn.
After the decision was announced, Trump cheered Huang’s return , insisting he had done nothing wrong and was a “genius” the country needed to power its AI boom and that there was no concern about his alleged romantic ties to Megaspeed executive Alice Haung (no relation).
“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security,” the president wrote on Truth Social Monday.
“The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
The Post argues that Hegseth’s alleged proposal reveals the “intensity” with which the military currently views the AI race with Beijing, as well as Silicon Valley ’s “growing entanglement” with the Department of Defense.

articles.title_orig: Musk makes $18 billion SpaceX stock pledge for every kid in America
articles.title_zh: Musk makes $18 billion SpaceX stock pledge for every kid in America
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account , and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active.
Musk said in a social media post on X on Thursday that the share from SpaceX would be transferred next month, without providing further details. "The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," he added.
Eligible children must have their account claimed to enable contributions from family members, friends and employers, and to receive the government's one-time $1,000 seed contribution. Auto-enrolled children can receive philanthropic contributions without a parent or guardian claiming an account, according to TrumpAccounts.gov.
Representatives for SpaceX and the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for further details about the planned gift.
SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell had previously agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts, with eligible account holders expected to receive them in December .
In October, Elon Musk posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year.
Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.
Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.
Since the July 4 launch, families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts . Total deposits now sit at more than $9 billion, CNBC first reported.
Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.
The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations , a move officials have said is meant to encourage more philanthropic gifts.
Contributing stock can benefit donors, who are able to avoid capital gains taxes triggered by selling appreciated stock. But families can face restrictions related to selling that donated stock. The policy also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.
Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17.
SpaceX shares have been under some pricing pressure as the company negotiates a possible merger with Elon Musk's automaker Tesla . The companies have established two special committees to handle merger negotiations, and hired advisers for a potential mega-deal.
CNBC's Sam Meredith, Kevin Breuninger, Kate Dore and Jess Dickler contributed to this story
