articles.title_orig: Chinese intel may have surveilled Alice Huang amid affair with Nvidia CEO, U.S. agencies tell Congress
articles.title_zh: Chinese intel may have surveilled Alice Huang amid affair with Nvidia CEO, U.S. agencies tell Congress
articles.content_orig:
China's Ministry of State Security may have been surveilling Alice Huang and sought information from her after her affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began, U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staffers Tuesday, according to people familiar with the briefing.
While there are still gaps in what U.S. intelligence agencies know, there is no indication to date that Alice Huang was specifically tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or that she passed information of significant value to the Chinese intelligence service.
But she was known to U.S. intelligence agencies to have been in contact with an MSS officer starting at least in spring 2025, multiple sources said, and her contacts with the agency raised counterintelligence concerns among U.S. intelligence officials. China's intelligence services rely not only on trained officers and formally recruited assets but also on citizens who are obliged under Chinese law to provide assistance when called upon.
Congressional staffers were also told that Kang Wei, believed to be Alice Huang's husband, had more extensive ties to the MSS, people familiar with the briefing said.
The New York Times was first to report on the briefing.
The two-hour briefing for House and Senate Intelligence Committee staffers, which included senior analysts from across the U.S. intelligence community, came two days after President Trump intervened to secure Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, despite national security concerns raised by some of his senior advisers.
Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under U.S. investigation for potentially diverting sensitive American technology to China.
Concerns about Alice Huang were laid out in a classified memo drafted this spring by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio that summarized U.S. intelligence, including intercepted communications involving the former Megaspeed executive. It was intended to ensure senior administration officials involved in relevant policy decisions were aware of the potential counterintelligence risks posed by her interactions with Jensen Huang.
Among those who received the memo were Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and senior White House staff. Rubio also briefed the president on intelligence.
The memo was not provided during Tuesday's briefing, despite requests from both congressional intelligence committees to see it.
China has denied allegations that Alice Huang is a spy.
Shortly after the existence of the memo came to light earlier this month, Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an extramarital affair. He later resigned as Nvidia CEO, but after less than two weeks, the company's board of directors reinstated him.
The reinstatement came after Trump administration officials offered Nvidia assurances that Jensen Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation and that the government had no legal issues with him, CBS News reported earlier Wednesday . The assurances did not extend to Alice Huang.
Two criminal investigations involving potential violations of U.S. export controls by Megaspeed and another buyer of Nvidia chips, Super Micro Computer, remain ongoing. The FBI has been investigating both cases for more than a year, with the Justice Department's National Security Division leading the Megaspeed investigation. Megaspeed has denied any violations of U.S. export control laws and says Alice Huang left the company last year.
Jensen Huang is expected on Capitol Hill next week for a closed-door session with House lawmakers and public testimony before the Senate Banking Committee.

articles.title_orig: Judges in Israel Suggest Dropping Key Corruption Case Against Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Judges in Israel Suggest Dropping Key Corruption Case Against Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.
The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.
The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.
In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.
"The chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.
The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case – concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 – met the threshold for criminality.
While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.
However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.
It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.
He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.
The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.
The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.
For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.
This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.
While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.
Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

articles.title_orig: China speeding up U.S. subversion, global expansion report warns
articles.title_zh: China speeding up U.S. subversion, global expansion report warns
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Minister of National Defence David McGuinty speaks during a meeting with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 22, 2025.
Canada’s Minister of National Defense David McGuinty on Tuesday emphasized his country’s sovereignty as he pushed back against the Pentagon’s accusation that Ottawa is falling short as a credible partner in defending North America.
"Canada's a sovereign nation. I'll be very direct. We don't report to the United States,” he told reporters, when asked about the Pentagon’s public rebuke. “I cannot explain the Pentagon's behavior, nor of the Secretary [of Defense.]”
The Pentagon under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released a two-page fact sheet on Monday, outlining what it described as Canada's “defense shortfalls” and criticizing the country's leadership under Prime Minister Mark Carney .
The document focused on what it characterized as Canada's underinvestment in the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and its defense spending plan for NATO. Canada joined allies at the 2025 NATO summit at the Hague in pledging to reach 5% of GDP by 2035 in defense spending. The country’s latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but Canada’s Parliamentary Budget Officer’s assessment last week stated that the path to reach 5% by 2035 remains “unclear.” The Pentagon, meanwhile, has accused Canada of deferring its largest increases needed to actualize the NATO spending target until after the 2029 federal election.
McGuinty staunchly defended his government’s defense spending plans, arguing that Canada remains on track to reach the 5% target. He argued that NATO allies had agreed to review the spending pledge in 2029.
When asked about the Pentagon’s comments that Canada is not a “credible partner,” McGuinty stressed the continued cooperation between the two neighboring countries.
"I can’t divine what the thinking is,” he added. “The amount of cooperation that we’re pursuing together under NORAD has not changed. What we’re doing together at NATO has not changed. Our military to military cooperation has not changed."
The Pentagon said Hegseth is “laser focused” on enabling Canada’s military modernization “after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its homeland defense.” The rhetoric follows that displayed by President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly accused Canada of “ ripping off ” the United States
Going a step further, the Pentagon also accused Canadian leaders of prioritizing domestic economic interests over military effectiveness, referencing Ottawa's ongoing review of its planned purchase of American-made F-35 fighter jets, arguing that the uncertainty surrounding the deal could undermine the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) cooperation. Carney ordered the review in March 2025, amid an escalating tariffs row and Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada and make it the “51st state.” The Pentagon said this review, along with Canada’s other alleged shortcomings, has prompted concerns as to whether the country can fulfill its commitments to NORAD, which is jointly operated by the two countries.
The Pentagon also questioned the readiness of Canada's military, claiming that only 41.9% of its air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%. The document framed these items as a burden on U.S. taxpayers.
Canada had previously emphasized its commitment to cooperating with the U.S. on matters of defense.
“As founding members of NATO, Canada and the United States have stood together in support of collective defense since 1949, and for nearly 70 years we have defended North America together through NORAD, the world’s only binational command,” a spokesperson for the office of McGuinty told TIME on Tuesday, prior to the minister’s comments to reporters. “Canada will continue to do its part to defend North America, as we keep having constructive discussions with our American partners on how best to strengthen our shared defense and security.”
Canada also announced over the weekend that it will join European NATO allies in exploring a pilot project in Keflavík, Iceland, as part of a proposed logistics network to support maritime patrols and anti-submarine operations in the North Atlantic and Arctic.
The move comes as Canada seeks to reduce its reliance on the U.S. by expanding its economic relationships and alliances with other countries. Carney has notably pursued a closer partnership with the European Union , and has laid out his vision for Canada becoming an “associate” member of the bloc. Both sides have expressed openness to a deeper cooperation in critical sectors including defense, technology, and AI.
While some of Canada’s international relationships are flourishing, the public tensions with the U.S. over defense priorities could have a negative impact on future alliances, experts argue.
“Our greatest advantages are the NATO and NORAD alliances, and we are looking to provide support to other partners,” says Andrea Charron, the director of the Centre for Defense and Security Studies at the University of Manitoba in Canada. “This kind of public shaming of a very close and important ally sends a chilling effect throughout all the allyships and partnerships that again serves no one but the adversaries.”
Typically, adversaries of the U.S. and Canada are “always looking for evidence of fractures in the allied relationship,” she adds, noting that now those people can “quote the Secretary of Defense.”
The release of the fact sheet follows a report by the Washington Post last week that said Hegseth had circulated a classified memorandum imposing new restrictions on military cooperation with Canada.
McGuinty responded to the report by saying he had not seen the memorandum and had no evidence of any changes to military cooperation between the two countries.
Joseph Jockel, a professor of Canadian studies at St. Lawrence University, says the noise around the memo regarding restrictions is “the second symbolic warning that [the U.S.] has sent Ottawa.” The first came in May, he says, when the Defense Department paused U.S. participation with Canada on the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD), a long-standing low profile mechanism for discussions on U.S.-Canada defense coordination.
“It sent a strong symbolic gesture, and now they're doing the same thing, they're looking for symbolic steps,” he argues.
Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, sought to downplay the significance of the reported restrictions, suggesting they were largely symbolic and would not affect day-to-day military operations, intelligence sharing, or defense planning.
“They’re basically limiting some social engagements, and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said at the Halifax International Security Forum on Nov. 21. “We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half.”
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told TIME that the Department of Defense “is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship."
“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence cooperation, our binational NORAD command, or our cooperation through NATO,” he added.
Despite those reassurances, the developments have raised concerns about the future of the countries' longstanding defense relationship.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said Sunday that any “restrictions on Canada-U.S. military cooperation by the Administration” would amount to a "terrible" mistake.
The Pentagon's public criticism of Canada's military capabilities and leadership comes as relations between the two countries remain strained by an ongoing trade war , with negotiations stalled and no clear path toward a

articles.title_orig: Iraq's top court says Baghdad can deploy troops to secure borders in Kurdistan region
articles.title_zh: Iraq's top court says Baghdad can deploy troops to secure borders in Kurdistan region
articles.content_orig:
Iraq’s top court has ruled that the federal government can deploy troops to the country’s international borders, including in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
Wednesday’s ruling comes a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal forces to take over Kurdish-run border crossings and demanded authority over oil fields controlled by Kurdish security forces, in an effort to curb oil smuggling.
Kurdish authorities denounced the move, with the regional government calling it “an assault” on the region’s “constitutional rights”.
The Federal ⁠⁠⁠⁠Supreme Court also ruled that federal authorities could oversee agencies operating at all border crossings, including those in northern Iraq’s Kurdish region, though they must coordinate with regional and provincial governments on customs administration, state television reported.
The court said the federal oil ministry can also oversee and audit oil and gas fields, while Baghdad shares responsibility for managing the oil and gas they produce with regional governments and producing provinces, according to state TV.
The Iraqi government did not specify how or when the takeover would be implemented.
The move comes just a week after al-Zaidi also took on Kataib Hezbollah – a powerful Shia militia aligned with Iran – following oil smuggling allegations.
He ordered troops to prepare to enter the city of Jurf al-Sakhar, a Kataib stronghold south of Baghdad. The group initially responded with defiance but allowed soldiers into the city, following a compromise brokered by Shia politicians.
The court’s decision appears to be a victory for al-Zaidi, but analysts say it will be challenging to implement moves against the Kurds and the heavily armed Shia militias loyal to Iran.
Renad Mansour, deputy director of the Middle East and ‌‌‌‌North Africa programme and director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, said Iraq’s judiciary was “very much supportive” of the government’s campaign to establish a centralised political order.
“The Iraqi government [is] trying to reclaim some sovereignty … because it’s such a fragmented state where there isn’t a centre,” he said.
A senior Shia politician close to Zaidi told the Reuters news agency that the prime minister was trying to dismantle the model of a “state within a state”. He added that al-Zaidi was trying to restrain armed factions operating above state authority, as well as draw clearer limits on the semi-autonomous Kurdish region’s exercise of authority over strategic economic and security matters.
The Kurdistan Regional Government on Wednesday rejected what it called “military ⁠⁠⁠⁠language and threats” in a statement from the Iraqi military announcing the new measures. It said ⁠⁠⁠⁠it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption and called for an end to oil smuggling across Iraq.
Iraq’s state news agency, citing what it said was a federal government intelligence report, said oil belonging to the state-owned North Oil Company was being diverted and smuggled from Kirkuk, as well as from Sulaimaniyah inside Iraq’s Kurdish region, to Iran and onward to Afghanistan.
Also on Wednesday, the Syrian and Iraqi defence ministers discussed “several issues of mutual interest” over the phone, according to Syria’s Ministry of Defence.

articles.title_orig: Why Nvidia's 'Jensen put' failed to stop the AI trade meltdown
articles.title_zh: Why Nvidia's 'Jensen put' failed to stop the AI trade meltdown
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO on Monday may have temporarily stabilized the AI trade, but it did little to fix the broader financial pressures weighing on markets.
Stock losses accelerated on Wednesday as Wall Street renewed its nervousness about the AI trade. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) shares tanked 6%, extending losses for a second consecutive session .
"It simply feels bad out there, and I'm not sure who's there to kick-save things at this current juncture into holiday illiquidity and zero tolerance for losses," Charlie McElligott, cross-asset macro strategist at Nomura, wrote in a note on Wednesday.
McElligott pointed out that the so-called Jensen put, or the idea that Huang's return can support the chip giant and the broader AI trade, does not address the tightening financial conditions in markets.
"What did Monday change? Not much!" the strategist said.
Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
On Monday, President Trump said he spoke to Nvidia's board members and "convinced" them to reinstate Huang 11 days after the CEO resigned amid reports of his affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia stock and the rest of the chip sector rallied hard on the announcement.
Despite the reinstatement, McElligott pointed to broader pressures facing markets, including higher interest rates, wider credit spreads, and heightened volatility, prompting investors to flock to cash and US Treasurys.
A squeeze on financial conditions leaves Nvidia and the broader AI trade vulnerable if another major setback emerges. According to an anonymous investor cited by McElligott, Huang's return has raised the stakes given greater scrutiny and congressional inquiries over the AI chip giant.
"This absolutely HAS to work," the investor said. "By that I mean he (Jensen) has to be 100% clean."
In other words, "if NVDA were to 'Go Wrong' again, we are left with an even higher cliff to jump from," McElligott wrote.
The AI trade has taken a substantial hit over the past month, with nearly every corner of the industry tumbling substantially. Nvidia stock is down roughly 30% over the past month and roughly 21% year to date.
Memory chipmaker Micron Technology ( MU ) is roughly 50% off its all-time high hit over the summer. Storage and memory-related stock Sandisk ( SNDK ) is down roughly 70% from its June record high.

articles.title_orig: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks
articles.title_zh: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stocks broadly slumped Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom.
The volatile day began with a sharp sell-off that briefly sent the influential Nasdaq 100 index into bear market territory, which occurs when an index falls by 20% or more from its most recent high. The S&P 500 was down by as much as 3.2% in early trading.
But sentiment among traders and investors improved slightly over the course of the day.
An early beneficiary of the renewed optimism was Anthropic, the AI giant that staged a record-setting IPO last week, only to see its stock battered for three straight trading sessions. Shortly after midday, Anthropic was finally trading back above its IPO price of $83 per share.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 1.5% and the S&P 500 was lower by only 0.5%. The Dow was flat in early afternoon trading and just barely back over a symbolic 50,000.
Even as markets pulled back from their lows, Nvidia remained among the biggest losers in key indexes.  After soaring by 31% on Monday on news that its recently-departed CEO Jensen Huang would return to the C-suite, the stock was still lower by about 7% Wednesday, its second straight down day.
The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption.
Stock markets Monday staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025, as the Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%.
President Donald Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang over the weekend despite multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Before the president stepped in, the board had been unequivocal that it did not plan to reinstate Huang.
Trump said Monday that he “probably” decided to intervene in Nvidia’s internal leadership decision because he was concerned about a market sell-off in the week after Huang’s departure fueled partly by investor concerns about how the CEO’s resignation would impact the broader AI industry.
But ever since Monday’s rally, markets have struggled to maintain that upward momentum.
“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note early Wednesday.
Before Monday’s one-day rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling, which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory on Friday, which is defined as a 10% drop from its last high.
Shares of semiconductor stocks, as tracked by the Philadelphia semiconductor index, have plunged more than 40% since their last peak in June. Stocks of companies that make data center and computer memory products have plummeted 60% over the same period.
AI-related sentiment has also been damaged further by frontier developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its initial public offering last week.
Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday.
Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold.
On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote.
On Wednesday, t he Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan and a dozen more.
“It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner wrote in a note Wednesday.
That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare-up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months.
Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.”
“Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs at Evercore ISI.
Compounding the negative pressure facing investors Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from its 2% goal.
The personal consumption expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month.
The rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy because it can indicate that higher gas prices sparked by the Iran war are spilling over into the rest of the economy.
It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision Dec. 9.
Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical.
“I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview . “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”
Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said.
A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs.
It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans and other forms of credit.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: The $2 trillion chip rally is getting wiped out — here's what history says comes next
articles.title_zh: The $2 trillion chip rally is getting wiped out — here's what history says comes next
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The biggest one-day rescue in stock market history is coming undone. Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, and Wall Street's AI doubts are back with a vengeance.
Monday was supposed to be the start of the comeback. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board brought Huang back at the White House's urging a week after chip stocks' worst week since 2001 , and the group added about $2 trillion in a day , a record $950 billion of it from Nvidia alone.
The sell-off since has hit the whole sector. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank nearly 8% Tuesday, with Micron ( MU ), AMD ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) down roughly 8% to 11% and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) off about 4%. On Wednesday, the index briefly dropped below last Friday's low, as Nvidia and Micron fell as much as 9% and 13%, before buyers stepped in and cut its loss to less than 1%.
The pain spread Wednesday morning, when the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell more than 3% and the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) nearly 5%. Dip buyers pushed both indexes back to small losses by the close, though Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) still finished lower.
Huang's return settled the question of who runs Nvidia. It didn't answer whether the debt-fueled AI-building boom will pay off, with tech borrowing costs climbing and the Fed still expected to raise rates on Dec. 9.
Sherwood News' Luke Kawa doesn't blame any single headline. "I think you can pin it on the sum of all the things that everyone's been pointing to for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang Tuesday.
Washington wants to help. President Trump told the New York Post a pardon for Huang is " always an option , I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." Asked about a government stake in Nvidia, he said, "It's probably not too late."
"I question what kind of a put it is," GammaRoad Capital Partners chief investment officer Jordan Rizzuto said. "I think it may be a very short-term put." Wednesday's new tariff proposal barely moved futures.
Turnaround Tuesday showed up on schedule. The next part of the script leans bearish. In the 20 times since 1993 that the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened a Monday 2% or more higher, it gave back at least half of that gain by Wednesday's close only five times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. SPY was on pace to join them Wednesday morning before a late rebound kept it out.
Every one of those fades went on to break the prior Friday's low within three months, most of them within a week. Of the 15 bounces that held up, only a third eventually broke the low in that span. Three of the drops came in the fall of 2008.
For the S&P 500, that low is about 6,883.
A year later, SPY was higher after 17 of those 20 big Monday rallies. In 2018, the Fed hiked into a nearly 20% drop and then paused, and stocks hit a record by April. Alfonso Peccatiello of the Macro Compass likes that echo but still sees more pain first, toward 6,500.
This Fed isn't in a position to blink . Wednesday's PCE report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed core prices up 3.3% from a year earlier, hotter than expected, making a December rate hike all but certain , with more possible early next year.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving. Advisors Capital Management's Gus Scacco expects Wall Street to wait on Huang's Senate testimony Dec. 3.
"We're going to probably be in purgatory here for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang .

articles.title_orig: China investigates Shanghai Party chief in latest blow to political elite - VOA
articles.title_zh: China investigates Shanghai Party chief in latest blow to political elite - VOA
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.
The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.
"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."
The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."
Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

articles.title_orig: They graduated college, but they haven’t been able to use their degrees
articles.title_zh: They graduated college, but they haven’t been able to use their degrees
articles.content_orig:
It's getting harder for college graduates to be optimistic about what's next after throwing their graduation caps in the air.
While unemployment among recent college graduates has been cooling as the job market has improved in the past few months, more and more graduates are having to settle for jobs that don't require the years of schooling they've just invested in. Based on data from the job-search platform Indeed, the share of bachelor's degree holders in jobs 12 months after graduation that don't require a college degree, or being underemployed, has risen dramatically in recent years.
Half of the class of 2025 were considered underemployed, above the 2017 to 2019 average of 39%.
Indeed economist Sneha Puri said the surge is due to the low-hire, low-fire job market that has been the story for the past few years. New grads also face a lot of competition for entry-level jobs. Puri said when employers do hire talent, they've been leaning on people "who can hit the ground running, as evident from the growth in job postings being driven by senior-level roles."
"That hits new graduates hardest, because they're most likely to apply for entry-level positions , which not only have seen job postings decline but also get several times as many applications as mid- and senior-level roles, including from people with more experience," Puri said.
Landing a job that doesn't require a college degree can be a short-term solution for new graduates, with long-term consequences.
"For workers who are underemployed or unemployed in their early years after graduating, that can have a stacking effect on their career over time, where they get knocked into a career trajectory that isn't as rewarding, isn't as engaging," Daniel Zhao, chief economist at Glassdoor, told Business Insider.
It could also affect their earning potential, as jobs that don't require degrees often pay less than those that do. For instance, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said there's no formal educational credential required to become a retail salesperson. That job paid an average annual wage of $37,310, per the latest 2025 BLS data, short of the overall average of $69,770. Software developers typically need a bachelor's degree, and Indeed said the average base salary for an entry-level software engineer in the US was about $82,000.
It can be tough to break free from underemployment.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Seventy-three percent of graduates who start out underemployed remain so 10 years after completing college , making them at that point about 3.5 times more likely to be underemployed compared with those who start out in a college-level job," a 2024 report from the Burning Glass Institute and Strada Institute said.
Zhao said there's also a risk for employers if they hire a college grad who isn't engaged in their work duties or who would be a better fit in a different position.
It can be easier to find a job in your field depending on your major. The New York Fed found, based on Census Bureau data, that criminal justice, performing arts, and fine arts majors had the top three underemployment rates in 2024. Nursing, aerospace engineering, and civil engineering made up the bottom three.
While computer engineering was among the majors with low underemployment, this major had the second-highest unemployment rate.
Puri expects underemployment to remain elevated for the class of 2026. "An uptick would only reverse once employers again start to recognize the importance of hiring and investing in entry-level talent to train tomorrow's senior level experts," she said.

articles.title_orig: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.title_zh: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

articles.content_orig:

Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday accused Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang of violating federal laws limiting advanced technology exports to China .
In a post on X, Schumer said Huang "shipped extremely advanced chips to China, violating US export control law, in what amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the Space Race."
Nvidia and the White House did not immediately comment.
Schumer's statement marked an escalation of congressional criticism against Huang, who was reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday despite claims regarding his relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese government agent. Lawmakers from both parties are increasingly questioning Nvidia's trade with China, pressing for tighter controls while investigating whether Huang's conduct endangered national security.
Lawmakers have also faulted President Donald Trump for pushing Nvidia to reinstate Huang as CEO.
Schumer and other legislators insist Congress must act rapidly to curtail American chip sales to China. Senator Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania Republican, said: "Congress must get to the bottom of what happened, and then strengthen our export controls to ensure China can't access our most advanced chips through the back door."
In a separate move on Tuesday, leading Democrats on four House committees wrote to Trump demanding answers about his awareness of Huang’s ties to the suspected agent.
"Your personal relationship with Mr. Huang and your willful blindness to the economic and national security risks posed by this scandal have put the American people at great risk," wrote Representatives Frank Pallone, Gregory Meeks, Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia, requesting all records of administration contact with the Nvidia board.
"Upon learning that Huang was in a relationship with a suspected agent of the Chinese government, what actions, if any, did Trump take to limit risks to America’s economic and national security?" the lawmakers inquired.
Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, told CNBC on Tuesday that more protections are needed on exports to China. "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang," he stated, adding it would be "just to make sure that he doesn't do something that is going to risk the United States."
Huang will appear on December 3 before the US Senate Banking Committee for a public hearing, panel's chair Tim Scott announced Monday.
Huang is also slated for a private briefing on December 1 with three House panels.
Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, said Huang's "reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake." He noted: "We sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law. That is a dangerous precedent to set."

articles.title_orig: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.title_zh: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.content_orig:
If we learned one thing form the browser wars of the 2000s, it’s that having a single ecosystem dominate the internet is best avoided. Yet here we are in 2026, and through Google’s Blink and Apple’s Webkit, we have very little diversity in the world of web browsing engines. Firefox is now very much an outsider, and that’s pretty much it. But there is another up-and-coming fully-featured browser, Ladybird, and it’s now available in alpha form for those of you with macOS or Linux.
This browser had an unlikely start, as a component of the esoteric operating system, SerenityOS. We tested it in that form and found it competent, but the process of running the OS in a VM, not so much. It was split into a separate project in 2024, and since then they have been working towards this point, of having something close to a release version.
We’ve followed Ladybird for a while now, not because we expect the world to adopt it en masse, but because, incredibly, it’s now the third major in-development browser engine family. Just as we needed the Konqueror-derived Webkit a couple of decades ago to provide a balance to the then-dominant Internet Explorer, we may need this piece of software at some point. We’ll give it a try, and perhaps you will too.
If only it had extensions (for my password manager+some random things) and userstyles and userscripts.
This makes me think that a good next target for an AI assisted software liberation would probably be web browsers. Yes, Firefox is open source, but the official releases are all run by a group of opinionated people who do it for a living. That financial support requirement understandably makes people conservative about taking risks. A modern AI assisted fork of any open source browser could do great things.
What great things exactly? I keep hearing about these great things but never what they are. Will they be as great as the slop that are those supposedly incredible apps that will kill Adobe?
Also lol about taking risks. What risks do you want to take? Firefox lost users exactly because it was “taking risks” and making stupid decisions.
An AI assisted fork will die as soon as it is released because nobody would give a shit about it.
“What great things exactly? I keep hearing about these great things but never what they are…”
Cat memes. The answer is reallly, really good cat memes.  That’s the whole point of AI…. Well… That and the extinction of the human species.
That sounds like a recipe for disaster honestly.
Browsers are undoubtedly the second most important thing besides the operating system itself and is through which nearly ALL our personal data goes including authentication data. The potential for disastrous consequences if there is any malice or neglect involved is incredibly high.
Trust isn’t to be given lightly with most serious browser forks and implementations taking ages to build rapport and the aspect of that those working on it are doing it for a living actually gives points in its favor. Trusting some random one-off AI Agent made fork among a flood of thousands of such: Seems like a very bad idea.
Good thing, then, that this isn’t a new project, and has a history that you can refer to.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as Huang comeback rally fizzles and AI concerns return
articles.content_orig:
Technology stocks fell on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1% and traded off its lows, recovering from steeper losses earlier in the session. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector edged down 2%.
"We just feel that this is panic right now," Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday.
"What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock," he added.
After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 5% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Marvell Technology and Intel all dropped about 2%, with some plunging further. Micron Technology declined 5%.
Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown.
Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle fell more than 4%. CoreWeave and Nebius moved lower.
AI lab Anthropic bucked the sell-off, however, and climbed more than 4% after shares dropped below last week's blockbuster IPO price.
Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech.
Amazon , Tesla and Alphabet each declined about 2%. Microsoft lost more than 1% and Meta traded higher.
